slides.theme: Open the door: welcome, the topic in one line, and what they'll get.
slides.script:
[walk to the middle, wait for the room to settle] Hi everyone, and thanks for coming. Thanks to [meetup name] for having me.

Tonight is about how my job changed. Not so long ago I was a developer who wrote code all day. These days I'm more of an AI builder. I decide what gets built, I hand the building to AI, and I check that it's right.

I'll keep this honest. No hype, no "AI will replace us all". You'll get how the role shifted, a video of me doing real work, and a trail you can follow starting tomorrow. [click]
slides.todo: Fill in [meetup name] on the cover and in the script.

slides.theme: Find out who's in the room and make the newcomers feel welcome.
slides.script:
Before we ride, a quick check. [ask for a show of hands] Who here writes code most days? [pause] Nice, most of you. Keep your hand up if AI writes most of that code for you. [pause] And who hasn't really started with AI yet? Be honest, nobody's grading you.

Good. That's pretty much the three groups on the screen. Developers, who write code and wonder what AI means for their job. Builders, who make things and want to make more, faster. And newcomers, who haven't started and maybe feel they've missed the wagon.

To the newcomers: you haven't. Honestly, starting now might even be an advantage, because you skip a lot of the clumsy early years. I'll come back to that later, I promise. [click]
slides.change: Drop the "Today I'm talking to: [..]" line from the slide.

slides.theme: Who's talking, in four short lines, ending on the shift.
slides.script:
So who am I? I'm Erik. I've done frontend and web development in Stockholm for a lot of years. Buttons, forms, layouts, the stuff people actually click on. I've always cared most about how things feel to use, and that hasn't changed.

I'm a consultant at Sigma Technology, and through Sigma I'm placed at Teneo. There I build Teneo X, a product where you build, test and run your own voice and chat agents. So I work with AI in the product, and with AI to build the product. Double dose.

And the shift: these days I call myself an AI generalist. AI is my engineering team. I'm the reviewer. [pause] That one sentence is pretty much what this talk is about. [click]
slides.change: Trimmed from 1:45 to 1:00. One line each: background, Sigma at Teneo, Teneo X, the shift. No company stats.
slides.todo: Add your photo to the WANTED poster on the about-me slide.

slides.theme: State the core idea plainly and let it land.
slides.script:
[read slowly] I used to write the code. Now I decide what gets built, and make sure it's right. [pause]

That's the whole shift. For most of my career, my value was in my fingers. How fast I could type out a solution, how well I knew my tools, how many shortcuts I had in my editor.

Today, the typing part is mostly done by AI. Not all of it, but most of it. What's left for me is the part on either side. Before: figuring out what the problem actually is, and what done looks like. After: checking that what came back is right, and good, and something I'd put my name on.

So the work didn't go away. It moved. And honestly, it got more interesting. From typing solutions to producing them. Defining problems, directing the AI, and judging the result. Let me show you what that looks like side by side. [click]

slides.theme: Make the change concrete, row by row, and reassure developers their skills still count.
slides.script:
Here's the before and after. I'll go row by row.

My main job. As a developer, I wrote the code. As an AI builder, I define the problem. Writing a clear problem turns out to be harder than writing the fix. If I can't explain it, the AI can't build it.

Where my time goes. It used to be implementing. Now it's instructing and reviewing. A lot of reading. More reading than I've done since school, honestly.

Who I work with. It used to be me and my editor. Now it's several AI agents at once, each on its own task. An agent is an AI that takes a task and works through it on its own, instead of just answering a question. Think of it as a small team that never gets tired and never gets bored, but also never pushes back unless you ask it to.

My value. It used to be how fast I build. Now it's what I choose to build, and taste. Knowing what's good and what isn't.

And what done means. It used to be: the code runs without errors. Now it's: it's verified, and it solves the actual problem. That's a higher bar, not a lower one. Code that runs but solves the wrong thing doesn't count anymore.

[pause] And to the developers in the room: none of your skills are wasted. Knowing how code works is exactly what lets me judge what the AI hands back. Without that, I'd just be nodding along.

[ask the room] Which of these rows already feels true for you? [let one or two people answer, then click]

slides.theme: A history lesson: the spinning jenny made spinning much faster, and people ended up working more, not less. My bet is AI goes the same way.
slides.script:
Quick history lesson. Around 1764, in England, a guy called James Hargreaves builds the spinning jenny. Before, one spinner worked one thread. Now one spinner runs eight at once. Later machines ran over a hundred.

So people worked less, right? [pause] Nope. A historian went through old court records, where witnesses mention what they were doing and when. Between 1750 and 1830 the working year got longer. About 15 to 30 percent. Mostly because people stopped taking Mondays off, and the holy days disappeared.

There's a name for this pattern. The Jevons paradox. Make something cheaper to use, and we often end up using more of it. Coal back then. Thread. Now, code.

And not everyone won. The handloom weavers lost out badly.

So this isn't a law of nature. It's my bet. AI makes building software cheaper, so we'll want a lot more of it. More things to build, and I think more people building them. [click]
slides.todo: Check you're happy with the bet framing: "more people building" is your guess, no source gives a head count. Check the hours range (15 to 30 percent, Voth's 14-32%) and the Monday/holy days line against the reading page.

slides.theme: Boil the new role down to three jobs and prime them to spot each one in the video.
slides.script:
If I boil the new role down, it's three jobs.

One: produce. That means deciding what problem is worth solving, and why. And owning the outcome, all the way from idea to shipped. If it breaks, it's on me, not on the AI. A lot of the time, the best call is deciding what not to build. The AI doesn't get the angry message in the morning. I do.

Two: instruct. Give the AI the context, the constraints, and a clear way to check the work. If I'd hand a new colleague a task, what would I tell them? Same thing here. The more vague I am, the more vague the result. Garbage in, very confident garbage out.

Three: bring taste. This is the hardest one to hand over. Looking at something that technically works and saying, no, that's not it. Pushing back. Cutting scope. Saying no when it isn't right. The AI will happily build anything you ask for. It has no sense of when to stop. You do.

[pause] Later on I'll show you a video of me fixing a small issue from start to finish. Watch for all three jobs in there. Where I decide what matters, where I instruct, and where I push back. [click]
slides.change: Replace "you saw all three in the demo" with: watch for all three in the video coming up.

slides.theme: The ground keeps shifting, so the job is mostly tinkering; one real story of a recent change.
slides.script:
And the ground under these jobs keeps moving. New models every few months. New tools. New ways of working. What worked six months ago may already be the slow way.

So most of my work is tinkering. [point at the loop] Try something new on a real task. Measure: did it save time, is the result better? Adjust the instructions or the model. Keep what works as the new default. Drop what doesn't, without feeling bad about it. Then a new model shows up and you go round again.

A recent example. A few weeks ago, one chat did one task. Now my main session works like a manager. It splits the work and hands pieces out to helper agents, little workers that each do one job and report back. Over two weeks, from mid September to early October, that was about five hundred handed-out tasks, with five to seven AI chats running at once on most weekdays. I also have a second laptop running extra AI accounts. One night it worked through a pile of review work. My to-do pile shrank while I slept.

For the power users: one night my agents closed all sixteen issues on a list and called it done. A second check the next morning found seven not fully fixed. Now a fresh agent reviews the work, never the one that wrote it.

My job in all that wasn't typing. It was deciding what to hand out, and checking what came back. [pause] And nobody has this figured out. Not me, not the big companies. That's what makes it fun. [click]
slides.change: Merged with the tinker slide: try, measure, adjust, refine, then a new model arrives and you go round again. Adds one real recent-change story (subagents as the team).

slides.theme: The working loop, define, direct, judge, and set up the video.
slides.script:
So what does this look like on a normal task? This is my working loop. Three steps, and I go round it many times a day, on tasks big and small.

Define. That's me. What's the problem, and how will we know it's solved? I agree on the check before anything gets built. Otherwise the AI decides when it's done, and it's very optimistic about that.

Direct. That's me and the AI together. We agree on a plan in small steps. Then the AI builds, and I steer. If it drifts off the plan, I pull it back. Small steps make that easy to spot.

Judge. That's me again. I review it with taste, I look at the proof that it works, and then it ships.

[pause] I own both ends of the loop. The AI does most of the middle.

In the video coming up, watch for those three. Define, direct, judge. [click]
slides.change: Now sets up the video: "watch for define, direct, judge".

slides.theme: A pre-recorded run of a real small task from issue to shipped, narrated live.
slides.script:
[before the video] This is a real task, just a small one. It's my own hobby project, a movie database app called emdb. It's public, so I can show you everything. The tool is [tool, e.g. Claude Code]. The task is an open issue, basically a to-do ticket: make the search look and feel better when you're using it. I recorded this so nobody has to watch me wait on wifi. [video starts]

[video: the GitHub issue "Search focused" with the two screenshots] Here's the issue. It's mostly two pictures. That's typical. Real issues are rarely a full spec.

[video: the issue pasted into the session, Erik asks it to suggest a check] First step is define. Before anything gets built, I ask: how do we know this is done? We agree on it. The search box gets a clear focused style, results show up the way the picture shows, and the app still builds and its automatic tests still pass.

[video: the AI writes a short plan in steps] Now direct. It proposes a plan in a few steps. I read it. I cut one step, because it wanted to touch the header too, and that's not this issue.

[video: files changing, terminal output scrolling] This is the AI building. This part I'll fast forward. It's honestly the least interesting part now.

[video: Erik looks at the result in the browser] Here's judge. It works. But the focus style is too loud, it looks like an error state. [video: Erik's pushback message] So I push back, one line: softer, use the accent colour, match the rest of the app.

[video: second version in the browser] Second try. That's the one. [video: build and checks passing] And here's the proof: the check we agreed on at the start passes.

[video: pull request, then the live site] A pull request, that's the change packaged up for review. Merged, and it's live on the web. [video ends]

[after the video] About four minutes, cut down from about [real duration]. My typing in all of that: a couple of sentences. My thinking: all of it. [click]

slides.theme: Plan mode: the AI reads the code and writes a plan, but changes nothing until I approve it. Define and direct, made concrete.
slides.script:
Remember the loop? Define, direct, judge. Here's a tool that makes the first two concrete. It's called plan mode.

In plan mode the AI reads the code, looks around and writes a plan. But it doesn't touch a single file until I say yes. In Claude Code you turn it on with Shift and Tab. Then you read the plan, and you can edit it before you approve.

So I see the route before we ride out. Not after.

Is it always worth it? No. It adds a step. If you could describe the change in one sentence, skip it. Use it when the change touches many files, when you're unsure how to do it, or when you don't know the code. [click]
slides.todo: If the demo video shows plan mode, say so here. Check the Shift+Tab shortcut still works in your version before the talk.

slides.theme: One bigger real example, the emdb revival, and where Erik stepped in.
slides.script:
That app you just saw in the video? Until a week ago it was a movie database I built back in 2020. Old technology, gathering dust.

On one evening, October fifth, I revived it. Moved it to modern technology, added new features, gave it a proper cinematic redesign, and put it live on the web. About an hour and forty minutes, start to finish.

Where did I step in? I decided what it should become. I set the bar for done. I said no to a couple of designs that looked generic. And I clicked through every page before it went live. The AI did the moving and the typing. I did the deciding and the checking. [click]
slides.change: One example only, no demo recap: the emdb revival.

slides.theme: A wanted board of things to build, with three Erik built himself.
slides.script:
Now let's get your imagination going. Here's a wanted board. Things you could build. Steal any of them as your first project.

A few of these I've built myself. [point] The personal dashboard. Mine has a view for work, a recap of what happened, and my tasks. I built it in one day, on September thirtieth.

[point] Review sheriff. It's a skill, basically a saved set of instructions, that reads the review comments on my pull requests, checks each one against the actual code, and fixes the ones that hold up. The ones that don't, it tells me why. That took about a day.

[point] Afternoon prototype. I needed a landing page, so I had three versions built in parallel, picked the best parts of each, and combined them. About two hours.

None of these are big. That's the point. Pick something small that annoys you. [click]
slides.change: Point out three he built himself: personal dashboard, review sheriff, afternoon prototype.

slides.theme: Reusable setups, with project memory walked through in detail.
slides.script:
Those were things to build. These are ways to set up the work. Recipes you can reuse every week.

I'll walk through one: project memory. It's a plain text file of rules that every AI session reads first. My conventions, how I like things done, what never to touch. So I don't have to explain myself every single morning.

The trick is keeping it short. I have one rule for that file: if removing a line wouldn't change the AI's behaviour, it's gone. No essays, no nice-to-knows. Every line has to earn its spot.

And one rule inside it that matters most: before anything gets built, we agree on a pass or fail check. A test, a command, something that says yes or no. That one line has saved me more time than any fancy tool.

For the power users: one line in my memory file says the AI may not touch a shared online database until I say a magic word. A small script also stops it and asks me. And no, I'm not telling you the word.

The others on the board, the parallel posse, spec first, the morning brief, are all worth a try. [click]
slides.change: Highlight one recipe: project memory, with the "if removing a line wouldn't change the AI's behaviour, it's gone" rule and a pass/fail check agreed before any build.

slides.theme: MCP: one standard plug that lets the AI use other tools and data, like a USB-C port for AI apps.
slides.script:
One more piece of setup. A lot of what I need lives outside my code. That's what MCP is for. Model Context Protocol. It's an open standard for connecting AI apps to other systems. Files, databases, search, design tools like Figma. The people behind it put it like this: think of it as a USB-C port for AI apps. One plug, lots of things fit.

A small connector program, called a server, sits in front of a tool and offers actions and data. Your AI app, like Claude Code, plugs into it.

An everyday example. Someone hands you a design in Figma. Plug in a Figma server, and the AI can look at the design itself, instead of you describing it.

For the power users: my AI's long-term memory is a folder of plain Obsidian notes, about three hundred of them. It writes everything it researches there, and searches it through its own MCP server. I even draw agent workflows as boxes and arrows, and it walks the drawing. [click]
slides.todo: Check the Figma example matches a server you've actually used, or swap in one you have. Optional if time allows: Anthropic introduced MCP in late 2024 and handed it to a fund under the Linux Foundation in December 2025.

slides.theme: Speak to the newcomers: it's not too late, start now.
slides.script:
Now, back to the newcomers. I promised.

[read the slide] Never worked with AI? You can saddle up today.

If you haven't really used AI in the last few years, that's fine. Here's the thing nobody tells you. A lot of what the early adopters learned is already outdated. All those tricks for coaxing a good answer out of a model in 2023? Most of them don't matter anymore. The tools got better and easier.

So the head start is smaller than it looks. If you start now, with today's tools, you can be as productive as someone who started years ago. Curiosity beats history here. You don't need to catch up on three years of hype. You just need to start with what's here today.

[pause] And for those of us who did start early: same goes for us. We have to keep relearning too. Nobody gets to sit still. [click]

slides.theme: Three simple steps to get going.
slides.script:
So how do you actually start? Three steps.

One: start small. One tool, one real task. Not a toy example, something you actually need done this week. Nothing fancy. Writing a test, cleaning up some messy code, drafting the intro doc for a project.

Two: feel it out. Try things. Notice what works and what doesn't. Adjust. You'll learn more from one real task than from ten tutorials.

Three: grow confidence. As you start trusting it on small things, take on bigger problems. Trust gets built the same way it does with a new colleague. A little at a time. And you'll find your own limits for what you hand over.

And when you ask it to do something, ask well. [click]

slides.theme: The four parts of a good instruction, using the emdb demo task as the example.
slides.script:
Here's what a good instruction looks like. It's the same thing you'd tell a colleague. These lines are from the video. Four parts.

Goal: make the search box clearly show when it's focused, and show results like the mockup.

Context: it's my movie app, and the issue has two screenshots.

Constraints: only touch the search, keep the app's colours, leave the header alone. That one stops it from wandering off and redesigning half the app.

And verification: the app still builds, the tests pass, and it matches the screenshots. [pause] This last one is the part people skip. It's also the part that makes the result something you can trust. [click]
slides.change: Replace the old "wrong order date" example lines with the emdb demo task. Goal: "Make the search box clearly show when it's focused, and show the results like the mockup in the issue." Context: "It's my movie app emdb. The issue has two screenshots of how it should look." Constraints: "Only touch the search. Keep the app's colours and fonts. Don't touch the header." Verification: "The build and existing tests pass, and the focused search and results match the screenshots."
slides.todo: Update the four example lines on the prompt-anatomy slide to the emdb task (see change).

slides.theme: Three habits of a trail boss, with one short story of being led astray.
slides.script:
Last, the mindset. Think like a trail boss. Treat the output as a draft. You own it. Once, the AI quietly locked in a default grocery store about 450 kilometres away. Prices and deals all came from the wrong shop. It looked right. It was wrong.

Iterate, don't restart. Say what's off and ask for another go. The second answer is usually better. And let it ask you questions first. End with "ask me anything you need first." It finds the gaps you missed. [click]
slides.change: Weave in the "led astray" story under "treat output as a draft" (default grocery store ~450 km away).

slides.theme: The big closing thought: the limit is what you can picture.
slides.script:
[read slowly] The only fence out here is your imagination. [pause]

What you can build now is limited mostly by what you can picture, and how clearly you can describe it. The typing isn't the bottleneck anymore. If you can picture it and explain it, you can probably build it. That was not true five years ago. So keep exploring, and keep learning. [click]

slides.theme: The call to action: one real problem this week.
slides.script:
So here's my ask. Start small. Keep exploring. Keep learning.

Pick one real problem this week. Define it, direct the AI, and judge the result yourself. Not a big one. A real one. Something that bugs you. And then come find me, or tell me online, what you tried. I'd genuinely like to hear it. [pause] Thank you. [click]

slides.theme: Thank-you and Q&A, with backup questions if the room is quiet.
slides.script:
Thank you so much. I've got about fifteen minutes for questions. Anything goes, including "that sounds terrible". [take questions; repeat each one out loud so everyone, and the recording, hears it]

[if quiet] A question I get a lot is...

Backup 1. What do I NOT use AI for? Deciding what's worth building, and the final yes or no on anything that ships. Also anything where I can't check the result, because then I can't judge it. And sometimes a two-line fix is just faster to type myself.

Backup 2. Doesn't this make juniors obsolete? I don't think so, but it changes how you learn. Juniors can ship much more, much earlier. The risk is skipping the understanding, so use AI to explain things, not just to do them. You still need to know how code works to judge it.

Backup 3. How do I check the AI's work? Same as a colleague's pull request. I agree on a check before it builds, a test or a command that says pass or fail. Then I read the diff, the list of changes, and click through the real thing. If I can't verify it, it doesn't ship.

Backup 4. What does it cost? [cost, e.g. a monthly subscription of around X per seat]. Compared to an hour of a developer's time, it pays for itself fast. Start on the cheapest plan and see if you hit the limits.

Backup 5. What about company code and privacy? Follow your company's rules first. That's not optional. Use business plans where your code isn't used for training, and never paste secrets or customer data. It's also why the video tonight used my own hobby project.

[when time's up] Thanks again. Slides and links are at [resource links], and you can reach me at [contact].

slides.theme: What is an LLM? Appendix TLDR plus link.
slides.script:
A large language model is trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next piece of text, again and again. It reads and writes in tokens: small chunks of words. The context window is its working memory. Underneath, it's a big file of numbers (the parameters) plus a small program that runs them.

Read more: https://erikpantzar.github.io/misc/work-in-progress/reading.html#llm
slides.todo: Check the TLDR reads well on screen.

slides.theme: How a model is made: data, pretraining, post-training. Appendix TLDR plus link.
slides.script:
Pretraining: the model reads a huge pile of text and learns to predict the next word. Post-training teaches it to follow instructions: fine-tuning on examples, then people ranking answers (RLHF). Anthropic also uses Constitutional AI, where the model gives feedback on its own answers from a written list of principles. The training data stops at a date, the knowledge cutoff.

Read more: https://erikpantzar.github.io/misc/work-in-progress/reading.html#training
slides.todo: Check the TLDR reads well on screen.

slides.theme: Weights and why model sizes differ. Appendix TLDR plus link.
slides.script:
Weights, or parameters, are the numbers a model learns in training. Models get better in a predictable way with more parameters, more data and more compute. Bigger models cost more to run, so labs also make small ones, for example by distillation: training a small model to copy a big one. Open-weight models are ones you can download and run yourself.

Read more: https://erikpantzar.github.io/misc/work-in-progress/reading.html#size
slides.todo: Check the TLDR reads well on screen.

slides.theme: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus and Fable: how models differ and how to pick. Appendix TLDR plus link.
slides.script:
Claude comes in tiers: Haiku is fastest and cheapest, Sonnet balances speed and intelligence, Opus is for long agentic coding and hard work, and Fable sits above it for the hardest reasoning. They also differ in speed, price per token and context window. Start with Opus for most work, or start cheap with Haiku and move up when tests show you need to. Compare models on your own tasks.

Read more: https://erikpantzar.github.io/misc/work-in-progress/reading.html#models
